summaries.example: Imagine a wooden door that was opened yesterday. A miracle might close the door today, but it would not make yesterday disappear. Damian used a similar idea: God could restore a person’s present condition without changing what happened in the past.
summaries.summary: Peter Damian was an eleventh-century religious leader and writer. His work On Divine Omnipotence asks two puzzling questions: Can God restore virginity to someone who has lost it? Can God make something that happened become something that never happened? Damian answered yes to the first question. He explained restoration as a present miracle: a person’s goodness or bodily condition could be restored, just as a door can be closed after it was opened. This does not erase the earlier event. For the second question, Damian’s main answer was no. He thought that making a past event both happen and not happen would be a contradiction, not a good thing. Since he defined omnipotence as the power to do anything good, this would not limit God’s power. A later, supplementary discussion says that God could have chosen a different history before events occurred, but that is different from changing the history that actually happened. Scholars disagree about how to read one famous passage, but the SEP entry says it does not justify claiming that Damian rejected the basic rule against contradictions.
key_ideas: Peter Damian wrote about God’s power in a work called On Divine Omnipotence.
He said God can restore virginity, understood as restoring a person’s goodness or bodily condition.
He did not need to say that God can erase the past.
Damian’s main view was that God cannot make a true event both happen and not happen.
Some readers misunderstood one difficult passage and thought Damian rejected basic logic.
Damian wanted people to speak carefully about God so that they would not wrongly think God is weak.
summaries.why_it_matters: Damian’s discussion shows how hard it can be to talk about unlimited power, time, miracles, and logic at once. It also teaches an important reading skill: one unclear passage should be compared with the writer’s other claims before we decide what the writer believes. His ideas helped shape later medieval discussions about possibility and necessity.

important_terms.definition: The claimed ability to do everything that is good. Damian did not think this required being able to do evil or nonsense.
The rule that the same thing cannot both be and not be at the same time in the same way.
A surprising event that goes beyond the usual rules of nature.
The idea that God’s plan includes all times and events in an unchanging way.

questions_to_think_about: Can fixing something now change what happened yesterday?
Is being unable to do something bad a weakness?
Why might a difficult sentence be understood in more than one way?

summaries.example: Suppose a court record truthfully says that an event occurred on Monday. A power to change the record today would not automatically make the Monday event not occur. Damian’s main approach treats “the event happened” and “the event did not happen” as incompatible descriptions. His supplementary approach instead considers a different possibility: God could have selected another providential history before this one existed.
summaries.summary: Peter Damian’s On Divine Omnipotence is an early medieval discussion of divine power, logical possibility, and time. Damian begins from a theological definition: God is omnipotent because God can bring about everything good that God can will. This does not require the ability to lie, do evil, or produce “nothing,” since those are not genuine achievements. It also does not require making contradictions true. Damian therefore answers the two central questions differently. He affirms that God can restore virginity, interpreting restoration either as renewed moral standing or as restored bodily integrity. On this account, restoration is a miracle in the present and does not remove the fact that the person previously lost virginity. The question of undoing the past is separate. In his main approach, Damian argues that past events remain past events within God’s immutable providential order. To make a completed event both have happened and not happened would be contradictory, and contradictory states are not included in omnipotence. He also discusses logical claims about what was, is, and will be, but does not fully explain the medieval debate about the necessity that follows from true statements. His supplementary approach uses a grammatical and temporal distinction: God could have chosen a different providential plan before the actual past occurred. That possibility is not the same as altering the past afterward. The SEP entry concludes that Damian’s reputation as a denier of non-contradiction rests too heavily on an ambiguous passage and conflicts with his broader argument.
key_ideas: Damian’s treatise addresses divine omnipotence through the questions of restoring virginity and undoing the past.
He distinguishes the power to do all good things from an alleged ability to do evil, make nothing, or actualize contradictions.
His main solution says the past cannot be undone because what God has made retains its status as having been made, and because God’s providential plan is immutable.
Restoring virginity need not involve changing the past: it can mean restoring moral standing or bodily integrity through a present miracle.
A difficult passage led some historians to portray Damian as rejecting the universal validity of non-contradiction, but the SEP entry finds that interpretation unsupported by the work as a whole.
Damian’s additional approach concerns what God could have chosen before time’s events unfolded, not a revision of the actual past.
summaries.why_it_matters: This case illustrates a major problem in interpreting historical philosophy: a provocative sentence may not represent a thinker’s settled position. Damian’s work also connects theology with modality—the study of possibility, necessity, and impossibility—and with questions about whether truth about the past creates necessity. His distinctions between present restoration, retrospective alteration, and an alternative original plan remain useful for analyzing claims about time and power.

important_terms.definition: In Damian’s account, God’s capacity to bring about anything good or anything God can rightly will; it does not include doing evil or producing contradictions.
The logical principle that one thing cannot both possess and lack the same property at the same time and in the same respect.
A necessity that follows from a fact’s being true, rather than a necessity that causes the fact to occur.
God’s unchanging plan or knowledge in which created events are held together beyond ordinary temporal change.
A theory of possibility and necessity: discussion of what must, may, or cannot be the case.
A restoration occurring within the present order of events, without removing the earlier event that made restoration necessary.
A state in which the same thing is required to be both the case and not the case in the same respect.

questions_to_think_about: What is the difference between changing a past event and choosing a different history from the beginning?
Does an inability to do evil count as a limitation on power? Why does Damian think it does not?
How does divine providence affect the question of whether the past can change?
Why might the distinction between a main argument and a supplementary argument matter when interpreting a text?

summaries.example: Think about a broken bicycle. Someone might repair it today, so that it works like a new bicycle. That repair does not mean the bicycle was never broken yesterday. Damian’s idea about restoring virginity works in a similar way: restoration can change a present condition without erasing the earlier event.
summaries.summary: Peter Damian was an eleventh-century monastic leader and Church reformer whose work On Divine Omnipotence became important in medieval philosophy. It discusses two linked-looking questions. First, can God restore virginity to a woman who has lost it? Second, can God make something that happened become something that never happened? Damian answers the first question affirmatively. He explains that restoration can mean returning to God and recovering moral standing, or repairing bodily integrity. In either case, restoration is a miracle happening now; it does not remove the fact that the earlier loss occurred. Damian’s main answer to the second question is negative. He treats undoing the past as requiring a contradiction: one event would both have happened and not happened. His definition of omnipotence avoids this problem. God can do anything good, but does not need to do evil, produce nothing, or make contradictions real. Damian also describes God’s providence as an unchanging plan in which past, present, and future are not obstacles in the way they are for human beings. Near the end, he gives an additional argument: before time began, God could have chosen a different order of events. Saying that God could have made a different past is not the same as changing the actual past. Later scholars have disagreed about the meaning of a difficult passage, but the SEP entry says it is too ambiguous to prove that Damian rejected the principle of non-contradiction.
key_ideas: Damian’s famous work grew from a discussion about whether God can restore virginity and whether God can undo the past.
He says restoration can concern a person’s moral condition or bodily integrity, and neither requires rewriting history.
His main answer is that God cannot make a completed event both happen and not happen.
He thinks this does not weaken omnipotence because contradictions and evil are not genuine good things to accomplish.
A controversial interpretation says Damian rejected basic logic, but the SEP entry explains why that reading does not fit much of the text.
In a secondary argument, Damian considers what God could have chosen before the actual sequence of events, not a change to the past after it happened.
summaries.why_it_matters: Damian’s questions help us see why philosophers distinguish possibility from actuality and restoration from reversal. They also show how religious arguments can involve logical ideas about contradiction, necessity, and time. His case is a reminder to read a whole work rather than build a major conclusion from one unclear passage.

important_terms.definition: The power to accomplish everything good that God can choose to accomplish, rather than the power to do evil or make contradictions true.
The idea that the same thing cannot both happen and not happen at the same time and in the same respect.
A change that goes beyond ordinary natural processes and is attributed to divine power.
The view that all times and events are included in God’s unchanging plan or knowledge.
A statement about what can happen, must happen, or cannot happen.
The condition of having been made or brought into existence by God.

Why does Damian separate the question of restoring virginity from the question of undoing the past?
